questions.prompt: What problem does home-grown management address first?
choices: Continuity across leadership change
Eliminating all outside hires
Reducing all experimentation

explanation.gentle: The chapter focuses first on preserving continuity when leaders change.
explanation.direct: Its opening concern is succession without institutional rupture.
explanation.competitive: It answers the panic that shows up when the chair changes hands.

questions.prompt: Why can an internal leadership pipeline matter in this chapter?
choices: It makes standards and judgment easier to carry forward
It guarantees that outsiders are always unnecessary
It removes the need for performance pressure

explanation.gentle: People developed inside the system can carry values, standards, and learned judgment more naturally.
explanation.direct: The chapter values internal pipelines because they preserve continuity through succession.
explanation.competitive: A real bench keeps the operating code inside the building.

questions.prompt: A company keeps needing famous outsiders whenever top roles open. What is the strongest chapter judgment?
choices: The company may be weak at reproducing leadership internally
The company has solved continuity perfectly
The company should stop building any internal pipeline

explanation.gentle: Repeated rescue hiring suggests the institution may not be generating enough continuity from within.
explanation.direct: The chapter reads constant dependence on outside saviors as a structural weakness.
explanation.competitive: If every transition needs a hero import, the machine is still thin.

questions.prompt: Elena's board is choosing between a celebrated outsider and a developed insider. Which response best fits the chapter?
choices: Choose only based on reputation
Judge who can carry the mission, standards, and learned judgment more reliably
Reject all insiders because they are too familiar

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants succession judged by continuity of purpose and competence, not by glamour alone.
explanation.direct: The right test is which option best preserves the institution's core through transition.
explanation.competitive: Make the bench prove it can carry the code, and make the outsider answer to the same demand.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the chapter's view of continuity?
choices: Continuity means copying old personalities exactly
Continuity means carrying the core forward through capable internal leaders
Continuity means never changing management roles

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants values and judgment carried forward, not personalities frozen in place.
explanation.direct: Home-grown management protects the institution's core rather than demanding imitation.
explanation.competitive: Pass on the operating logic, not the mannerisms.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main failure mode for internal pipelines?
choices: Stale insularity and comfort-based promotion
Too much external prestige
Excessive experimental learning

explanation.gentle: Internal pipelines can go wrong if they reward familiarity instead of competence.
explanation.direct: The danger is continuity turning into a shelter for insiders rather than a carrier of standards.
explanation.competitive: Comfort can wear a succession badge and still rot the bench.

questions.prompt: A school club keeps improvising officers at the end of each year. What question best applies the chapter?
choices: How can the club prepare successors earlier so continuity survives turnover?
How can the club depend more on one charismatic leader?
How can the club stop teaching future officers anything?

explanation.gentle: The chapter would ask how the group can build continuity by developing future leaders in advance.
explanation.direct: Early successor development is the school version of home-grown management.
explanation.competitive: If turnover wipes the memory every year, the bench is missing.

questions.prompt: Which sign most strongly suggests that an internal pipeline is healthy?
choices: Insiders are promoted mainly because they are familiar
Future leaders are carrying the core forward while still being tested for competence
No one ever questions succession choices

explanation.gentle: A healthy pipeline preserves continuity without dropping standards.
explanation.direct: The chapter wants internal development tied to excellence as well as to cultural continuity.
explanation.competitive: The bench is real when it carries the code and still has to earn the chair.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 8 follow the experimentation chapter so naturally?
choices: Because internal leaders can help preserve learned judgment across transitions
Because experiments remove the need for managers
Because outside hires erase all prior learning automatically

explanation.gentle: The chapter follows experimentation by asking who can carry those lessons forward over time.
explanation.direct: Leadership continuity helps keep earlier learning from evaporating at succession points.
explanation.competitive: A company that learns through trials still needs a bench that remembers.

questions.prompt: What question naturally follows this chapter according to its bridge forward?
choices: What standard keeps continuity from settling into complacency?
Why should the company stop setting standards altogether?
How can all management be outsourced?

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks what performance standard keeps continuity from going soft.
explanation.direct: After continuity, the book turns toward relentless standards.
explanation.competitive: The bench is built. Next comes what keeps it hungry.
